title: Why New Orleans jazz died: lost social use and no one paying
summary: Rose says jazz outlived its social use. In old New Orleans music was communal, with picnics and family bands, so no one paid for it and musicians left.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: That's not the reason why it died, though. Well. The reason why it died is because of the fact that it literally outlived its social utility. It literally no longer met the emotional needs of its audience.
And could you describe what those were a little bit?

Well, of course, the attitudes in New Orleans in the time when it came up were first a completely good time attitude on a communal basis. What happened was that we would go out to the lakefront for picnics and bring a band along, and everybody listened to the band, and the band had a good time playing together. And nobody was trying to be a star, and nobody was trying to achieve individual recognition with the general public. They were satisfied to be known as the best band around.
Okay, Al, let me just interject this. Why, then, did things get to the point in New Orleans where musicians couldn't find work, they had to leave, and also...
I'll tell you one main reason for it.
But they had a tremendous competitive atmosphere, which sounds like it wasn't...

Well, one of the main reasons why the musicians left New Orleans is a very simple one. And that is that as much as New Orleans people loved jazz, and they always did love jazz, they never felt a need to spend any money for it. One reason was because of the fact that there are such an enormous lot of people who can play jazz in New Orleans. There are so many families who have their own bands, right, in a family, you see? Everybody played. That's a consideration. People played, you know, in the old days without air conditioning. People used to go out in a neutral ground with guitars and ukuleles, and they would play and sing and have a hell of a time. When I was a kid, I didn't know a single family that didn't have a piano in the living room, and at least two or three people in the house could play it. So the music was in the air, and it was so common. I mean, like, we all appreciate air, but we don't fight with each other over who's going to breathe the most of us.
It was taken completely for granted.
That's right. Not only taken completely for granted, but it was literally common in the sense that everybody played it.
So when the question of who's going to pay for it becomes a necessary question, that spells the end of it.

That's right. Not only that, but we have, even today, I mean, we have a lot of old men in New Orleans who are very prominent socially and heads of big organizations who are, at the same time, were well-known jazz musicians in New Orleans. Are they supporting it? Well, they don't even think in terms of supporting it. I mean, if they feel like playing it, they play it. But the point is that it wouldn't occur to them.
So another reason it's dying out is because there's no one left to play it.
That's one of the main reasons, sure. To fill the roles. Nobody left to fill the roles of the musician in the jazz band.
